text.p: Slovakia, one of the former east bloc countries seeking NATO membership, welcomed on Thursday a pact between NATO and Russia as a milestone towards stability in Europe.

A brief statement issued in Bratislava by Slovak Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik, currently in Warsaw, said that although the text of the accord reached on Wednesday was not yet known the fact that it had been reached was a good sign for Europe.
"We expect that the agreement between Russia and NATO will be one of the important steps on the path towards achieving stable relations and an atmosphere of confidence in Europe," Hamzik said.

The deal with Moscow outlining a new political and military relationship allows the U.S.-led North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) to proceed with plans for its eastwards expansion into former communist Europe.

In return, Moscow gets a permanent voice at the centre of Europe's security order which critics say its diminished status no longer merits and that it will misuse to undermine the rights of smaller nations.
Slovakia is one of the Eastern Europe countries striving to join western economic and political structures after the break- up of the Warsaw Pact seven years ago.
However its chances of being invited to join in the first wave appear slim after repeated U.S. and European Union criticism of the pace of democratic reform.
Slovakia is to hold a referendum on whether to join NATO, along with another on whether to introduce direct presidential elections, on May 23-24.

The government-sponsored referendum on NATO membership comprises three questions - are you in favour of NATO membership, are you in favour of the deployment of nuclear missiles in Slovakia and are you in favour of the establishment of military bases in Slovakia.

The opposition has accused Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's government of deliberately confusing the issue with the inclusion of the second and third questions. It says they are deliberately phrased to elicit a vote against membership, thereby providing the government with an alibi in case Slovakia is not invited to join the alliance.

Slovak President Michal Kovac and leaders of opposition parties have appealed to the population to vote "yes" to NATO membership and to direct presidential elections and to ignore the questions on nuclear weapons and bases.
